prompt: With an asynchronous standby, the primary confirms a commit and dies a millisecond later. What happens to that commit if the standby is promoted?

choices.text: It is replayed from the primary's memory
choices.why: The primary is dead; its memory went with it.

choices.text: It is safe, because a commit is written twice
choices.why: Written twice on the primary's own disk, not on the standby's.

choices.text: Lost, if the log had not reached the standby
choices.why: Right. The application was told yes about a transaction the new primary never received.

choices.text: The standby refuses to be promoted
choices.why: Nothing in promotion checks for commits it never saw.

prompt: Order the values of `synchronous_commit` from the one that returns soonest to the one that waits longest.
hint: Follow the commit from the primary's memory to the standby's data.
trap: remote_write and on both wait for the standby; on also waits for its disk.

prompt: Match each setting, with a synchronous standby, to the moment the commit returns.

pairs.right: It is on the primary's disk
The standby has written it, not flushed it
The standby has flushed it to disk

prompt: `synchronous_standby_names` is empty. What does `synchronous_commit = on` wait for?

choices.text: Its own disk, as local does
choices.why: Right. With no synchronous standby, on and local behave the same.

choices.text: Every connected standby to flush
choices.why: Only standbys named in synchronous_standby_names are waited for.

choices.text: The first standby to connect
choices.why: An empty list names nobody.

choices.text: Nothing; it behaves like off
choices.why: on still waits for the primary's own flush.

prompt: One database records payments and page views. What does the lesson suggest?
hint: The setting is not only server-wide.

choices.text: Two servers, one for each kind of data
choices.why: Possible, but the setting already lets one server do both.

choices.text: remote_apply for the server, to be safe
choices.why: Then every page view pays the cost of a payment.

choices.text: off for the server, and a nightly dump
choices.why: Payments would lose their last second of commits on a crash.

choices.text: Choose synchronous_commit per transaction
choices.why: Right: remote_apply where losing the commit matters, off or local where it does not.

prompt: What does the primary compare with the names in `synchronous_standby_names`?
hint: Each standby says it when it connects.

choices.text: The standby's port number
choices.why: Ports are not names; both standbys could use the same port on different hosts.

choices.text: Its application_name
choices.why: Right. Here it is set in the connection string pg_basebackup copied into primary_conninfo.

choices.text: The name of the standby's cluster
choices.why: Lesson 11's standby reported 16/standby only because nothing else was given.

choices.text: The replication slot's name
choices.why: The slot is separate; the list matches application_name.

prompt: A standby introduces itself with the `___` in its `primary_conninfo`, and the primary lists it under that name in `pg_stat_replication`.
hint: Two words joined by an underscore.

prompt: Why does this lesson pass `-d 'host=... application_name=standby1'` to `pg_basebackup`?

choices.text: pg_basebackup refuses to run without a name
choices.why: Lesson 11 ran it without one.

choices.text: -R copies the string into primary_conninfo
choices.why: Right, so the standby uses the name every time it connects.

choices.text: The slot is named after the application
choices.why: The slot is named by -S.

choices.text: It makes the copy synchronous
choices.why: Nothing is synchronous until the primary's synchronous_standby_names names it.

prompt: In the lesson's run, average latency was 1.610 ms with the standby asynchronous and 1.969 ms synchronous. How many milliseconds did each transaction pay for the wait?
Why does the lesson call its measured cost the cheapest synchronous replication will ever be?

choices.text: pgbench runs faster than real applications
choices.why: The workload is not the point; the distance is.

choices.text: The standby had no queries of its own to serve
choices.why: That helps a little; the round trip is what grows.

choices.text: PostgreSQL 16 removed the network wait
choices.why: Every synchronous commit waits for one round trip.

choices.text: The standby is on the same machine
choices.why: Right. Every real standby adds a network round trip to each commit.

prompt: An import commits one million rows one at a time against a synchronous standby with a 100 ms round trip. Ignoring everything else, how many hours does the waiting add?
What does `synchronous_commit = off` risk?
hint: It does not wait for the primary's disk either.

choices.text: Recent commits, if it crashes
choices.why: Right: the last fraction of a second of them, on a crash of the primary, with or without a standby.

choices.text: The standby falling hours behind
choices.why: Replication is unaffected; the risk is on the primary.

choices.text: Corruption of the data files
choices.why: off loses recent commits; it never corrupts the database.

choices.text: Nothing, if there is a synchronous standby
choices.why: The primary may still lose commits it confirmed before writing them.

prompt: `synchronous_standby_names = 'standby1'` and standby1 stops. What happens to writes on the primary?

choices.text: They continue asynchronously
choices.why: PostgreSQL never downgrades on its own; that would break the guarantee silently.

choices.text: They fail at once with an error
choices.why: They wait, with no error and no end.

choices.text: They wait until the standby is back or the setting changes
choices.why: Right. The primary does not fall back to asynchronous by itself.

choices.text: The primary shuts down
choices.why: It keeps running and keeps waiting.

prompt: While the `INSERT` waited on `SyncRep`, another session counted the order and got 0. Why?
hint: The commit is on the primary's disk.

choices.text: The insert had not been written yet
choices.why: It was written and flushed on the primary before the wait.

choices.text: The other session read from the standby
choices.why: Both sessions were on the primary.

choices.text: count(*) skips rows from the last second
choices.why: count has no such rule.

choices.text: A waiting commit is invisible to others
choices.why: Right: until the wait ends, nobody else sees it.

prompt: What did `statement_timeout = 3s` do to the insert waiting for the stopped standby?

choices.text: Cancelled it after three seconds
choices.why: timeout killed the client at ten seconds; the database never cancelled it.

choices.text: Rolled it back on the primary
choices.why: It was already committed locally.

choices.text: Nothing at all
choices.why: Right: the statement had finished, and the commit waits outside the statement.

choices.text: Made the primary go asynchronous
choices.why: No setting on a connection changes the server's replication.

prompt: A session waiting on `SyncRep` is cancelled. What is in the table, and what does its client see?

choices.text: On the primary only; INSERT 0 1
choices.why: Right: the row is on the primary only, and the client got a warning and then INSERT 0 1: success, on a row that exists on one server. An application reading only INSERT 0 1 never knows.

choices.text: No row, and an error
choices.why: The commit happened before the wait and cannot be undone.

choices.text: No row, and INSERT 0 1
choices.why: The row is there: the count was 1.

choices.text: The row on both servers, and a warning
choices.why: The standby was stopped; it has nothing.

prompt: What did `exit 124` mean in the lesson's transcripts?
hint: It is the exit status of one of the commands.

choices.text: The insert violated a constraint
choices.why: That would print an ERROR from psql.

choices.text: timeout killed psql after ten seconds
choices.why: Right: the command was still waiting when the limit arrived.

choices.text: The standby refused the connection
choices.why: psql connected to the primary, not the standby.

choices.text: psql lost the connection to the server
choices.why: That exits with 2 and prints a message.

prompt: With `ANY 1 (standby1, standby2)`, standby1 stops. What happens to the next insert?

choices.text: It waits for standby1 to return
choices.why: That is what a single named standby does.

choices.text: It commits asynchronously, with a warning
choices.why: standby2 confirmed it; nothing became asynchronous.

choices.text: It commits, confirmed by standby2
choices.why: Right: exit 0 at once, and the commit is still on two servers.

choices.text: It fails until the list is edited
choices.why: The quorum is exactly what avoids that.

prompt: Match each value of `synchronous_standby_names` to what a commit waits for.

pairs.right: standby1, and stops when it is gone
standby1 while it is connected, else standby2
Whichever of the two answers first

prompt: How many PostgreSQL servers, primary included, does it take for every confirmed commit to be on two machines while one standby can fail without stopping writes?
hint: One primary and a quorum of one out of how many?

prompt: One standby is in the same data centre and one in another city. Why might a team choose `FIRST 1 (near, far)` over `ANY 1 (near, far)`?
hint: Which does each one wait for in steady state?

choices.text: It states a preference for near
choices.why: Right: the far one is only waited for when the near one is gone, which makes the slowdown predictable and visible.

choices.text: FIRST is faster when both are up
choices.why: ANY waits for the quickest, which is at least as fast.

choices.text: ANY needs both standbys to be up
choices.why: ANY 1 needs one.

choices.text: FIRST keeps the far standby asynchronous forever
choices.why: It becomes the synchronous one when near is gone.

prompt: A shop agreed to an RPO of a few seconds for orders, and has one standby. What does this lesson suggest?

choices.text: Make the one standby synchronous
choices.why: Then the standby's failure stops every order.

choices.text: synchronous_commit = off, for speed
choices.why: That loses commits on a crash of the primary itself.

choices.text: Synchronous, plus a timeout on every statement
choices.why: A timeout does not bound the commit's wait.

choices.text: Asynchronous, with its lag watched
choices.why: Right: seconds of RPO need no synchronous standby, and its failure stops nothing.

prompt: A payment table is protected by `ANY 1` over two nearby synchronous standbys. Somebody runs `DELETE FROM payments` without a `WHERE`. What gets the rows back?
hint: Synchronous replication copies faster; it does not judge.

choices.text: Promoting one of the standbys
choices.why: Both standbys replayed the delete, sooner than an asynchronous one would.

choices.text: A point-in-time restore
choices.why: Right: point-in-time recovery from the archive to a moment before the delete, as in lesson 6. Replication protects machines, not data.

choices.text: Cancelling the delete's SyncRep wait
choices.why: The delete was committed on the primary before the wait.

choices.text: Nothing: it cannot be recovered
choices.why: The base backup and the archive can bring back the moment before.
